title: AQ Podcast | Keiko Fujimori Takes Power. Can She Keep It?
gist: Episode summary page for an Americas Quarterly podcast with former Peruvian Finance Minister Alfredo Thorne, framing Keiko Fujimori's July 28 inauguration as Peru's ninth president in ten years, won by under a percentage point, against a backdrop of a doubled homicide rate and 3.4% growth widely seen as below potential. No transcript is present, so only the page's own framing claims are captured.

themes.theme: Peru's presidential instability and a thin mandate

insights.claim: Keiko Fujimori took office on July 28, 2026 as Peru's ninth president in ten years, a succession in which most predecessors' terms ended in impeachment, resignation or prison.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: Nine presidents in a decade is the base rate for Peruvian executive turnover — assume elevated probability that this term also ends early when pricing multi-year Peruvian policy continuity.
insights.quote: On July 28th, Keiko Fujimori took office as Peru’s ninth president in ten years. Most of her predecessors’ terms ended in impeachment, resignation, or prison.
insights.locator: On July 28th, Keiko Fujimori took office

insights.claim: Fujimori won Peru's June runoff by close to 50,000 votes, less than a full percentage point ahead of leftist Roberto Sánchez, and opposition lawmakers walked out of Congress rather than hear her inaugural address.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: A sub-1pp margin plus an opposition walkout on day one signals immediate governability risk and a low bar for congressional obstruction of reform.
insights.quote: Opposition lawmakers walked out of Congress rather than hear her inaugural address.
insights.locator: She won a June runoff by close to 50,000 votes

insights.claim: Peru's homicide rate has doubled in recent years, which is why Fujimori's campaign message of stability, security and economic reform resonated with voters.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: A doubled homicide rate makes security policy the dominant political variable in Peru — expect security spending and enforcement measures to lead the agenda over economic reform.
insights.quote: a message that resonated in a country where the homicide rate has doubled in recent years

insights.claim: Peru's economy grew 3.4% last year but is widely regarded as still far from its potential, framing the growth-unlock question for the new administration.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: A 3.4% print with acknowledged slack sets the baseline against which any Fujimori reform agenda — or El Niño drag — will be measured.
insights.quote: despite growing 3.4% last year, is still far from its potential

insights.claim: The central open questions posed for Fujimori's term are whether she can deliver stability after a decade of chaos, unlock Peru's economic potential, and navigate the country's relationship with both Washington and Beijing.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: The U.S.-China balancing act matters for Peruvian mining and port concessions — watch how the new government handles Chinese-linked infrastructure.
insights.quote: we ask whether Keiko Fujimori can bring stability after a decade of chaos, unlock Peru’s economic potential, and navigate the country’s relationship with Washington and Beijing

insights.claim: Alberto Fujimori's legacy — stabilizing Peru's economy and defeating the Shining Path in the 1990s before being imprisoned for human rights abuses and corruption — is explicitly framed as the shadow over his daughter's presidency.
insights.speaker: Americas Quarterly
insights.so_what: The father's dual record sets the two tail scenarios investors should hold for this term: hard-line stabilization or institutional erosion.
insights.quote: Alberto Fujimori stabilized Peru’s economy and defeated the Shining Path in the 1990s, but was later imprisoned for human rights abuses and corruption.
